transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-10
Start time (UTC): 15:30
Duration: 1:12
Attendees: Sofia Martinez (Redwood AE), Daniel Cho (Redwood SE), Alex Rivera (Lead ML Eng, Cisionware), Priya Nair (Platform Eng), James Holt (CTO)

Summary: intermittent oscillating throughput observed on Cisionware private deployment during bursts. Hypotheses: continuous-batching window misconfiguration, aggressive token caps, or KV cache thrash. Today: triage, propose quick knob matrix and bench plan.

Topics: scheduler knobs, continuous batching windows, max_num_seqs, token_limit, KV hit-rate, quantization tradeoffs, VPC NIC/NVLINK considerations.

--- Transcript (timestamps approximate, transcription imperfect) ---
[00:00:00] Sofia (AE): Hi everyone, thanks for carving the time, um we'll try to keep this focused. Quick intros?
[00:00:08] Alex: Alex here, lead ML eng at Cisionware — we run a bunch of customer-facing generative workflows, have a private VPC deployment with Redwood dedicated nodes.
[00:00:12] Priya: Priya, platform — I mostly own infra and observability.
[00:00:16] James: James, CTO — I'll listen for the big tradeoffs.
[00:00:20] Daniel (SE): Daniel, Redwood SE — I did the initial config review, looking forward to pairing on knobs.
[00:00:25] Sofia: Cool. Quick framing: Alex pinged us about oscillating throughput during peak windows — sometimes throughput drops 30–50% for a minute then recovers. Looks like scheduler behavior plus cache misses. Daniel, you want to start with the traces?
[00:00:36] Daniel: Yeah. So from the traces Alex shared, the timeline shows continuous batching queues growing, then a sudden shift — lots of small sequences dominate and the scheduler seems to switch to a conservative path. There's also a KV hit-rate dip at the same time — looks like eviction pressure.
[00:00:49] Alex: Right, we saw p50 latency go up and token throughput fall. Logs show increased eviction events and more GPU memcpy spikes. Not sure if it's NVLINK or the model's kv-storage thrash.
[00:01:02] Priya: One thing — we run a mixed workload, short chat completions and longer summarizations. The short chats spike at 60 reqs/sec then die, so it's very peaky.
[00:01:12] Sofia: That mixed profile is classic for continuous-batching misalignment. Quick note: our runtime will try to pack sequences up to max_num_seqs, but when the arrival distribution changes it may end up with many small seqs which increases kernel overhead.
[00:01:25] Daniel: Exactly. The scheduler has a few knobs — continuous_batching.window_ms, max_num_seqs, token_limit_per_req, and priority windowing. If the window is too short, you get many flushes; if too long, latency tail suffers.
[00:01:40] [00:01:41] Alex: We currently have continuous_batching.window_ms=20, max_num_seqs=16, token_limit_per_req=2048.
[00:01:47] Daniel: That window is kinda small for your burst pattern; with 20ms we might flush before enough sequences coalesce. Also, max_num_seqs=16 can cause lots of micro-batches when many small requests come in.
[00:01:58] Sofia: Another signal — KV cache hit-rate drop. When lots of unique prefixes show up, kv hits drop, we fetch from host memory more, causing memcpy pressure. If KV eviction churns, token generation slows.
[00:02:10] Priya: Any best-practice numbers? We were planning to keep token_limit high to avoid truncation.
[00:02:15] Daniel: Tradeoff: higher token_limit_per_req lets long requests through but also increases steady-state memory per sequence which reduces effective slot count. For peaky short workloads you can set a conservative token_limit (e.g., 1024) and enable prefix caching for common prompts.
[00:02:29] Daniel: Also, one trick is to increase max_num_seqs to 24 or 32 for throughput, but pair it with a token_floor or token_ceiling so extremely long requests don't starve.
[00:02:40] [00:02:42] Alex: We tried max_num_seqs=32 once and saw lower latency p50 but then noticed p99 spikes. Not sure why.
[00:02:48] Daniel: That could be due to head-of-line blocking — long requests included in a big batch can delay other short ones if priority windows aren't set. We have a priority windowing feature that reserves X slots for short sequences — have you enabled it?
[00:03:00] Alex: No, not yet.
[00:03:02] Sofia: We'll propose a knob matrix: increase window_ms to 50–80ms, try max_num_seqs at 24, add a short-seq reservation (priority window) of 20% of batch slots, and lower token_limit to 1024 for short-mode.
[00:03:16] James: What about KV cache sizing? Is it a memory knob?
[00:03:20] Daniel: KV cache is proportional to num_slots * avg_seq_len. On GPUs with limited HBM you can push to host-cache which costs memcpy. For private deployments we recommend pre-warm (KV prefetch) if you have predictable prefixes; otherwise bump the KV cache quota or use eviction_policy LRU tuned to favor recent sessions.
[00:03:36] Priya: We're on A100s with 40GB HBM and a small host-side reserve. Sometimes during the spike the host->gpu transfers saturate NVLINK. I saw kernel busy but also memcpy stalls.
[00:03:47] Daniel: That aligns: if KV hit-rate dips, every token generation may cause page-in from host memory. Small batches exacerbate memcpy overhead due to more frequent transfers.
[00:03:58] [00:04:00] Alex: So practical plan — run three bench permutations and watch KV hit-rate, memcpy bytes, and scheduler flush frequency?
[00:04:07] Daniel: Yes. Permutations: A) window_ms=20, max_num_seqs=16 (current baseline), B) window_ms=60, max_num_seqs=24, priority_reserved=20%, token_limit=1024, C) same as B but max_num_seqs=48 to stress test.
[00:04:21] Sofia: Also try quantization changes — INT8 reduces memory per activation and could increase effective slot capacity. But watch for quality regressions on your summarization model.
[00:04:31] Alex: We're using an LLaMA derivative — quant int8 is on the table; we worry about small quality drop on legal doc summaries.
[00:04:38] Daniel: Then run a quick eval set of e.g., 50 prompts to check Rouge/EM or your eval metric alongside perf runs. The goal is to see token/sec improvements vs any perf regression.
[00:04:48] Priya: One weird symptom — the runtime sometimes switches model variant during fallback and that correlates with throughput drops. Could that be routing?
[00:04:55] Daniel: Could be. Smart routing may fallback to a lower-memory variant if capacity is constrained; ensure model pinning for Dedicated nodes or configure fallback policy off for the pilot test.
[00:05:07] Alex: We'll pin model version for the bench.
[00:05:10] [00:05:12] James: Network? Any possibility it's external network or control plane making changes?
[00:05:15] Priya: We've seen ephemeral spikes on the subnet but nothing that lines up perfectly. The correlation with KV eviction looks strong.
[00:05:22] Daniel: For VPC/on-prem, watch for NIC queue saturation and NVLINK metrics. We'll add recommended perf counters to the runbook.
[00:05:30] Sofia: Ok let's walk through a quick runbook snippet live — Daniel?
[00:05:34] Daniel: Sure. Step 1: enable verbose scheduler logs (trace level), collect batch composition histograms (seq lengths per batch), continuous_batching.window_ms and flush counts. Step 2: record KV hit-rate and eviction events per minute. Step 3: collect GPU memcpy counters (host->gpu bytes) and nvlink utilization. Step 4: run bench permutations A/B/C for 10 minutes each with steady synthetic traffic plus burst patterns.
[00:06:02] Alex: For synthetic traffic, any recommended arrival distribution?
[00:06:05] Daniel: Do a Poisson baseline at your steady qps, then add a 30s burst with 3x qps. Also replay a sample of real requests if possible.
[00:06:15] [00:06:18] Priya: On the continuous_batching.window_ms change — are there guardrails so latency doesn't blow up for interactive requests?
[00:06:22] Daniel: Yes, priority short-window ensures interactive gets reserved slots; also you can set max_latency_ms per route so the runtime forces an early flush for interactive endpoints.
[00:06:32] Alex: Anything else about token caps? We have some callers sending 6k tokens occasionally.
[00:06:36] Daniel: Big single requests are killers for batching. Use token_limit_per_req to cap, or route long-form completions to a different queue with lower concurrency but higher slot allocation.
[00:06:45] Sofia: Also note autoscaler and burst capacity — if you can burst nodes to absorb high concurrency periods it helps, but there's a cost. For now, we'll optimize the knobs before autoscaling changes.
[00:06:56] James: I want an executive summary — what's the minimal change to try first?
[00:07:00] Sofia: Increase continuous_batching.window_ms to 50–60ms, set max_num_seqs to 24, enable 20% short-seq reservation, lower token_limit for the interactive route to 1024. That should address most of the oscillation.
[00:07:12] Alex: Ok we'll run that as B. If that fails we try C and then look at quantization.
[00:07:18] Daniel: I'll attach the runbook steps and a small script to toggle knobs via the config API. Also include commands to dump histograms and KV metrics.
[00:07:26] Priya: For the bench environment — do you need access to logs or remote tracing?
[00:07:30] Daniel: Prefer logs uploaded to the shared sheet; for deeper traces we can provide a temporary support token to pull diagnostic traces.
[00:07:37] Alex: We'll start with logs.
[00:07:40] [00:07:42] Sofia: Any blockers on compliance or security for sharing these traces?
[00:07:45] Priya: We need to scrub PII; we can sanitize and share.
[00:07:48] Sofia: Good.
[00:07:50] Daniel: Quick note on quantization: INT8 can reduce HBM by ~30–40% for activations; sometimes that converts a host-transfer heavy workload to mostly HBM resident, improving token throughput. But again, evaluate quality.
[00:08:04] Alex: We'll include eval set.
[00:08:07] Daniel: Also check CPU usage on the host — sometimes copying and kernel launch overhead move to CPU threads and that matters if you have pinned CPUs.
[00:08:15] Priya: We saw CPU spike during the memcpys.
[00:08:18] Daniel: Then include CPU counters in the collection set.
[00:08:21] [00:08:24] James: Last question — are there any Redwood-managed defaults that could be surprising?
[00:08:28] Sofia: Default runtime sets continuous_batching.window_ms=30 and max_num_seqs=16 for safety across workloads. For production of peaky workloads we often recommend custom tuning like we discussed.
[00:08:40] Alex: That explains a lot.
[00:08:41] [00:08:44] Sofia: Ok recap — Daniel will send the knob matrix, a small script, and the runbook. Cisionware runs three bench permutations and shares sanitized logs and the eval results. We'll meet next week to review.
[00:08:58] Daniel: I'll also include a short checklist for KV pre-warm and an optional INT8 quality test harness.
[00:09:05] Alex: Thanks everyone.
[00:09:07] Priya: Thanks.
[00:09:08] James: Appreciate it.
[00:09:10] Sofia: End.
